uncited: This method aggregates complementary geometric and appearance information from multiple camera views to enhance the radiance field representation of dynamic humans.
It combines time-augmented skeletal features, which provide robust geometric priors via a SMPL model, with pixel-aligned image features, which capture high-frequency visual details.

*   **Inputs:** A 3D query point $x \in \mathbb{R}^3$ in world space; a set of $C$ input images $I_{c,t}$ at time $t$; camera parameters for each view; a SMPL model instance at time $t$; and the viewing direction $d \in \mathbb{R}^3$.
*   **Skeletal Features ($s^0_{c,t}$):** A dense 3D volume of features $d$-dimensional, defined on the SMPL mesh vertices and interpolated into space.
*   **Pixel-aligned Features ($p^x_{c,t}$):** A $d$-dimensional feature vector extracted from the image $I_{c,t}$ corresponding to the 2D projection of $x$.
*   **Attention Weights ($mv\_att^x$):** A $C \times C$ matrix representing cross-view compatibility.
Map the query point $x$ to the local coordinate space of the SMPL model at time $t$.
This feature is time-augmented, encoding geometric deviations of the SMPL vertices.
Project the query point $x$ onto the 2D image plane of each camera view $c$ to obtain pixel coordinates.
Sample the feature $p^x_{c,t}$ from the image $I_{c,t}$ at these coordinates.
Let $s^0_{1:C,t} = \{s^0_{c,t} \mid c=1,\dots,C\}$ and $p^x_{1:C,t} = \{p^x_{c,t} \mid c=1,\dots,C\}$ be the sets of skeletal and pixel-aligned features across all $C$ views.
Compute keys $k(\cdot)$ and values $v(\cdot)$ for both feature types using learned linear layers (independent from temporal transformers).
This highlights confident observations where skeletal and image features are compatible.
Here, $z^x_{c,t} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the view-wise representation for view $c$.
Compute the mean of the pixel-aligned values across views: $\bar{v}_p = \frac{1}{C} \sum_{c=1}^{C} v(p^x_{c,t})$.
Apply positional encoding $\gamma_d(d)$ to the viewing direction $d$ (using $2 \times l$ basis functions as in [28]).
The attention mechanism mitigates this by down-weighting incompatible views, but extreme occlusion may require robust skeletal priors.
*   **SMPL Accuracy:** The skeletal feature retrieval depends on the accuracy of the SMPL pose estimation.
*   **Time Complexity:** Dominated by the multi-view attention mechanism, which is $O(C^2 \cdot d)$ for the attention weights and $O(C \cdot d)$ for the aggregation, plus the MLP inference.
The SparseConvNet sampling is efficient due to sparsity.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Requires storing the SparseConvNet volume for skeletal features and the image features for all views.
Handles multi-view inconsistencies via attention.
Improves rendering quality for articulated humans.
Computationally more expensive than standard NeRF due to multi-view processing and attention.
*   **When to use:** Dynamic human rendering where multi-view consistency and geometric priors are beneficial.
*   **When not to use:** Static scenes without articulated subjects, or resource-constrained environments where SMPL inference and multi-view attention are too costly.
The method originates from the "Neural Human Performer" paper, which introduces a framework for learning generalizable radiance fields for human performance rendering.
